Jim Lebenthal bought more Alphabet (GOOGL) after a 14% monthly slide, calling it "a correction, not something worse."

QQQ and SPY fell 11% and 6% in a month yet remain up for the year, so the correction label fits indexes better than Alphabet.

Cloud revenue doubled and powers the shots-on-goal case, but negative free cash flow, heavy borrowing and stock sales are Alphabet's weak spot.

Read: Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps with, and it is free today. Read more here.

Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) closed at $273.10 on Nov. 25, down 13.79% in a month. Jim Lebenthal used the drop to buy more. On CNBC's Halftime Report, the show's regular said: "The call is that this is a correction, not something worse. Not the AI bubble popping. And if that's the case, then this is the buying opportunity."

24/7 Wall St.

He also argued that Alphabet has many ways to win: "Whether it's the search, the chips, the Gemini model, whether it's YouTube, whether it's Waymo. I've got a lot of shots on goal here, so why not add to it?" Market data and Alphabet's filings test both claims.

GOOGL Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
Correction Label Fits the Indexes Better Than Alphabet

A correction usually means a drop of 10% or more. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) fell 10.99% over the past month. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) fell 6.36%. Both are still up for the year, at 3.19% and 5.1%. That looks like a correction.

Alphabet's own decline runs deeper. The stock is down 12.58% year to date and 15.34% over the past year. It also sits about 21.5% below the $348.10 it traded at when it filed its second-quarter results on July 22. Investors are marking down Alphabet more than the market.

title: $2,000,000 In QQQ At The 2000 Peak Ran Out

Trefis Team

Image from Pixabay

If you plan to retire soon and most of your savings sit in tech funds, this autumn has been hard to watch. Invesco QQQ, the fund that tracks the Nasdaq 100 index, closed at $633.93 on Wednesday, Nov 25. That is 16.6% below its record close on Oct 6.

We tested what past tech falls did to a retirement plan held all in QQQ. In our five tests since 2007, the plan sat through falls of 23.3% to 56.7% in dollars, and each time it got back. In a sixth test, from 2000, the money never came back. $2,000,000 all in QQQ at the March 2000 record, with $80,000 taken out a year, ran out on Jul 1, 2008. It lasted 8.3 years.

What happened to an all-QQQ retirement that began at the 2000 peak?

Every test uses the same plan. It puts $2,000,000 in at a Nasdaq 100 high close. It takes out a fixed $80,000 a year, which is 4% of the start, in monthly amounts. The amount is not raised for inflation. Dividends are reinvested, and taxes are left out.

From the Mar 27, 2000 record, the Nasdaq 100 fell 82.9% to its October 2002 low. By then the QQQ plan was worth $243,477. After 100 monthly withdrawals, $666,204 in all, nothing was left.

QQQ took a retirement that began at its 2000 peak down to zero by Jul 1, 2008. If your monthly bills come out of your savings, selling shares deep in a fall is what empties the account. The Trefis Income Solution owns 50 companies that have each paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row, and together they yield about 3 times what the S&P 500 pays. See the Income Solution.

How close is this fall to a tech bear market?

At its Nov 20 low, the Nasdaq 100 was 19.8% below its Oct 6 record. That is just short of a 20% fall, the usual line for a bear market. The index has crossed that line 5 times since 1999. Those falls began in 2000, 2018, 2020, 2021 and 2025. The 2007-2009 fall is not counted on its own, because the index had not yet got back to its 2000 record.

The slide has not gone in one direction. QQQ fell 2.0% on Tuesday, Nov 24. It fell another 0.65% on Wednesday, Nov 25. Even so, it closed 4.2% above its Nov 20 low. Three of the 23 days since October 2011 when the Nasdaq 100 moved 5% or more came this month.

How did each mix hold up in past tech falls?

The table sets an all-QQQ plan against a mix of 60% VOO, the S&P 500 fund, and 40% BND, a broad bond fund. Each row starts at a Nasdaq 100 high and follows the same plan. The mix is set back to 60/40 at each withdrawal. Before VOO began in September 2010, the tests use SPY, another S&P 500 fund.
